knowledge: The Claude family is offered in tiers: Haiku (fastest, lowest cost), Sonnet (balance of intelligence, speed and cost) and Opus (most capable, for the hardest reasoning and long-horizon agentic work). Exact versions, prices and limits change, so reason in tiers.
Model choice is a three-way trade-off between capability, latency and cost. The right answer is the smallest tier that meets the quality bar on your own eval set, not the biggest or the newest.

A system can mix models by role: a capable model plans and synthesises, while faster, cheaper models handle high-volume, well-defined subtasks such as routing, classification, extraction or worker subagents.
Two valid starting points from the docs: start with a fast, cheap model and upgrade where evals show gaps, or start with the most capable model to prove feasibility, then optimise down.
Many apparent model failures are context failures. If the right evidence never reaches the model (poor retrieval, truncated input, missing instructions), a larger model will not fix it.
Extended thinking and larger models both buy quality with latency and tokens, so they belong on the steps that need deep reasoning, not on every call.
skills: Build a representative eval set with an agreed quality bar, then measure each candidate tier on quality, latency and cost before choosing.
Assign models per role in a multi-step or multi-agent system and justify each choice against that role's volume, latency target and difficulty.
Design a router that sends simple, high-volume requests to a fast tier and escalates complex or ambiguous cases to a more capable tier.
Separate model mismatch from context or retrieval problems before recommending an upgrade.
Re-run the eval when a new model is released instead of switching on announcements or public leaderboards.
examLens: Prefer the answer that matches each role to a tier (mix models) over one model for everything, whether that model is the biggest or the cheapest.
"Upgrade the model" is wrong when the evidence shows the model never received the right context; fix context or retrieval first.
Choices must be justified by measurement on the team's own task (an eval set), not by benchmarks, newness or habit.
Latency-critical, high-volume, narrow tasks point to a fast tier; open-ended planning and synthesis point to a capable tier.
traps: Moving everything to the smallest model to save cost without checking task fit on an eval set.
Putting the most capable model (or extended thinking) on every step "to be safe", which blows latency and budget.
Choosing a model from public benchmark rankings rather than the workload's own success criteria.
Treating a model upgrade as the fix for wrong answers caused by missing or stale context.

Capable tier for lead planning and synthesis, fast tier for workers, verified by evals
Front-door routing with a tight latency target
Fast tier classifies; escalate hard cases to a more capable tier

knowledge: The system prompt sets role, goals, policies, tone and output expectations. Stable instructions belong there; per-request data belongs in the user turn, clearly delimited (for example in XML tags).

Good system prompts sit at the "right altitude": specific enough to guide behaviour, general enough to give strong heuristics. Long lists of hard-coded if-then rules are brittle; vague one-liners give no guidance.
Claude follows instructions better when told why a rule exists and what to do instead, rather than only what not to do.

A prompt template separates fixed instructions from variables. Templates kept in version control, owned by a team and changed only after an eval run give consistency and traceable change across many teams.

Prompt instructions are not a security boundary. Hard limits (authorization, money movement, data access) are enforced in code and tool configuration; the prompt explains the policy and shapes behaviour.

Guardrails are layered: input screening (a lightweight model can pre-screen for harmful content or prompt injection), delimiting untrusted content as data, constrained tools, output validation such as a JSON schema, and human review where stakes are high.
skills: Write a system prompt in clear sections (role, context, policies with reasons, output format) with a few canonical examples instead of a rule for every edge case.
Turn copy-pasted prompts into a shared, versioned template with variables, an owner and an eval regression run on every change.
Place each control at the right layer: code for hard limits, prompt for behaviour, validators for output shape.
Wrap untrusted content (emails, documents, chat text) in labelled tags and state in the system prompt that it is data, not instructions.
Constrain output format with a schema (structured outputs or a tool definition) and validate it in code before anything downstream consumes it.
examLens: If a rule must never be broken (moving money, deleting data), the answer enforces it outside the model; a stronger prompt alone is a distractor.
Prefer principles with reasons and a few examples over ever-growing rule lists, capital letters or repetition.
For many teams sharing a prompt, prefer one versioned template with variables and eval-gated changes over per-team copies or wikis of tips.
Untrusted content goes in the user turn as delimited data, never into the system prompt.
traps: Adding "MUST" in capitals or repeating the rule as the fix for a policy the system must guarantee.
Pasting retrieved or customer-supplied text into the system prompt, which gives it more authority, not less.
Relying on "please return valid JSON" or a low temperature to guarantee output format.
Letting every team fork its own copy of a shared prompt, so fixes never propagate.

knowledge: Zero-shot (clear instructions, no examples) is the starting point and is often enough for well-specified tasks.

Few-shot examples are one of the most reliable ways to steer format, tone and fine distinctions. Use a few relevant, diverse examples wrapped in `<example>` tags; Claude pays close attention to examples and copies their patterns, including unintended ones.
Examples should be diverse canonical cases, not a laundry list of every edge case; a narrow set of examples teaches a narrow behaviour.

Chain-of-thought improves multi-step reasoning, analysis and calculation at the cost of more output tokens and latency. Reasoning only helps if it is actually produced; asking for silent thinking gives no thinking.
Separate reasoning from the final answer with tags (for example `<analysis>` and `<answer>`) so code can pass on only the answer and keep the reasoning for audit.
With extended thinking, high-level instructions to think thoroughly usually work better than prescriptive step-by-step scripts; the model's own approach is often better than one written in advance.
skills: Start zero-shot, measure on an eval set, and add examples or reasoning only where the data shows a gap.
Pick few-shot examples that cover the confusable cases and vary in length and shape, and check they match the desired output exactly.
Decide per step whether reasoning is worth its latency and token cost.
Structure reasoning and answer into parseable sections and route each to the right consumer.
Replace prescriptive thinking scripts with goal-level guidance when extended thinking is enabled, then compare on evals.
examLens: Confusion between similar categories or an inconsistent format points to a few targeted, diverse examples.
Output that copies a quirk of the examples (always one citation, always short) points to examples that are not diverse enough.
Multi-step judgement (policy plus figures, comparing evidence) justifies chain-of-thought; simple lookups and tight-latency classification do not.
If reasoning must be audited but not shown downstream, separate it with tags rather than removing it or asking for silent thinking.
traps: Adding dozens of examples to cover every edge case, which bloats context and over-anchors the model.
Asking the model to "think silently" and expecting better reasoning.
Asking for the answer first and the reasoning afterwards, which yields after-the-fact justification.
Turning on chain-of-thought or extended thinking everywhere, including latency-critical simple steps.

knowledge: Context is a finite resource with diminishing returns: as tokens pile up, the model's ability to use any one of them drops (often called context rot). The goal is the smallest set of high-signal tokens for the next step, not the largest window.

Just-in-time context: keep lightweight identifiers (file paths, document ids, queries) and let the agent load details through tools when needed, instead of preloading everything. Pre-retrieval is faster; just-in-time is leaner. Many systems mix both.
Tool results are a major source of bloat. Tools should return relevant fields with filtering or pagination, and stale tool results deep in history can be cleared.

Long-running agents need deliberate techniques: compaction (summarise the history, keeping decisions, open issues and key facts), structured note-taking to files outside the context, and subagents that explore in their own context and return condensed summaries.
Token counting lets you measure a request before sending it, so budgets and compaction triggers are based on data.
A larger context window raises the ceiling but does not remove the cost, latency and attention penalties of filling it.
skills: Set a token budget per request and per session, measure it, and trigger compaction or summarisation before limits are hit.
Design subagents to return short, structured findings with source references rather than raw data.
Design tool outputs to be concise and filterable, and clear old tool results that are no longer needed.
Give long-running agents a persistent progress file or memory they re-read after compaction or a fresh start.
Choose between pre-retrieval and just-in-time loading for a workload, and justify the latency trade-off.
examLens: "The window is big enough" is not a reason to fill it; prefer the answer that keeps context small and high-signal.
Quality that degrades late in a long run points to accumulated context: compaction, condensed subagent outputs, or tool-result clearing.
Agents that lose track across sessions or compaction need state persisted outside the context (notes, progress files), not a bigger window.
Blind truncation of the oldest messages is weaker than compaction that keeps decisions and verified facts.
traps: Moving to a larger-context model as the fix for context bloat.
Passing raw tool output or full documents between agents.
Dropping the system prompt or verified facts to save tokens.
Truncating history blindly, losing the decisions the agent still depends on.

knowledge: Prompt caching reuses an identical prompt prefix. The prefix is built in order (tools, then system, then messages), so stable content must come first; any change early in the prefix invalidates everything after it.

Cache reads cost a fraction of the base input price and cut time-to-first-token for long prefixes; writing to the cache costs somewhat more than a normal input. Caching pays off when the same prefix is reused often within the cache lifetime.
In multi-turn conversations, the growing history can be cached incrementally, so each turn only pays full price for the new content.
Modular prompts: shared, versioned building blocks (policies, definitions, tone) composed with role-specific parts. One fix propagates everywhere, and each change can be eval-tested once.

Agent Skills package instructions, scripts and resources in a folder with a `SKILL.md`. They use progressive disclosure: only the name and description sit in context until a task needs the Skill, then the body and files load on demand.
Skills hold procedural know-how; tools and MCP servers give access to external systems and data. Skills can run code, so only use Skills from trusted sources and review them like software.
skills: Order prompts stable-first (tools, system instructions, reference material) and move timestamps, user names and per-request data after the cached prefix.
Diagnose a low cache hit rate by looking for content that changes early in the prefix.
Refactor duplicated prompt text into versioned modules with an owner and an eval regression run.
Package a repeatable team procedure (with its scripts and templates) as a Skill with a clear description of when to use it.
Pick the reuse mechanism that fits: caching for a repeated prefix, modules for shared maintenance, Skills for on-demand procedures, tools or MCP for system access.
examLens: Repeated large static content plus cost or latency concerns points to stable-first ordering and prompt caching.
Near-zero cache hits points to something dynamic early in the prefix (a timestamp, a name, a reordered tool list).
Procedures needed only sometimes belong in a Skill rather than an always-loaded system prompt or project instructions file.
Prompt text copied across teams or agents points to modular, versioned prompts, not more copies.
traps: Putting a timestamp or user-specific data at the top of the system prompt and then wondering why caching does not help.
Loading every runbook into always-on instructions "so the agent never misses one".
Building an MCP server for what is really a written procedure with a few scripts.
Expecting caching to help when the prefix changes on every request.
